h1: Developing a core beer range for a new market
title: A core beer range for a new market | Craft Beer School
desc: How to choose a first range of beers for a market you are entering: local drinkers, climate, food, water, price and a sensible number of beers.
teaser: Four good beers beat ten average ones. This is how to choose them for a market you do not yet know.
standfirst: A core range is the few beers you brew all year. Choosing it for a new market means learning what drinkers there want and what your plant can make well.
sections: Start with the drinker, not the style

Visit bars, shops and restaurants in the target market. Note which beers sell, at what price, in what serving format and at what temperature. Ask staff what customers ask for. Taste local competitors closely. Learn what flavours the market already enjoys and what it has not been offered.

Write down three things about the market before designing a recipe: what people drink now, what they pay and where they drink it. If you cannot answer all three, you need more visits before you brew.

In hot climates, drinkers want cold, refreshing beer. A well made lager or pale ale usually leads. In cooler places, richer styles sell in colder months. Think about where the beer is drunk: outdoors, with food or at a taproom. See designing a lager for hot countries for how heat affects recipe choices.

Local food shapes taste as well. Where meals are spicy, light lagers and wheat beers do well. Where grilled meat is common, amber lagers fit. Our pairing guides, such as Southeast Asian food, show how this works.

Your local water shapes what you can make. Soft water suits pale lagers. Water with high carbonate needs correction for pale beers. Desalinated water has almost no calcium or magnesium, so minerals have to be added. Have a full water analysis done. Check what malt and hops you can get, how long they take to arrive and how you will store them in the local climate.

Think about transport too. Beer that travels in hot vehicles ages faster, so a hop-forward beer may suit a taproom better than a long distribution chain. A malt-led lager often travels better.

For a new brewery or a new market, three to five beers is enough. A common mix is:

  • An approachable lager or pilsner as the volume leader.
  • A pale ale or wheat beer with more flavour.
  • A darker or stronger beer for variety.
  • A seasonal or rotating slot to keep interest.
  • A non-alcoholic option, where it fits the market and the law.

Each additional beer adds tanks, yeast handling, packaging changes and stock. Keep the range tight until sales justify more.

Think of the range as a set of jobs. The lager brings in new drinkers, the pale ale rewards the curious and the dark beer gives regulars something to explore. If two beers do the same job, drop one.

Alcohol duty is often tied to strength, so a beer a point lower in ABV can change the economics. Rules vary by country and change, so check with your national regulator or a licensing adviser. Decide your formats early: keg for bars, can for retail and bottle where the market prefers it. Each format has its own shelf life.

Think about shelf life. If distribution is slow or storage is warm, a beer that peaks fresh may disappoint by the time it reaches the glass. Plan stock rotation and date coding from the start.

Run small test batches and let real drinkers taste them. Ask simple questions: would you buy it, what would you pay and what would you drink it with. Treat the answers as data and not as a verdict. Make notes of sensory feedback with a consistent form. This is where tracking the right numbers begins.

A pop-up tasting or a limited run at a local venue gives feedback before you commit to tanks. Collect comments the same way each time, using a short form with a score and three words.

A first range is a hypothesis. After six months of sales, look at what sold and what sat. Retire beers that do not move and develop new ones from what drinkers asked for. Our consultant brewers can review a draft range with you by video: costs, recipes and what your equipment can do. See also commissioning from overseas if equipment is part of the plan.

Cost each beer before launch. Grain, hops, yeast, packaging, energy and labour differ by recipe. A beer that looks good on the menu may lose money on the tank.
faqs: How many beers should a new brewery launch with?
Three to five is usually enough. Each extra beer adds cost and complexity.
Should the first beer be a lager?
Often, because lager is the most widely accepted style and rewards clean brewing. Check the local market first.
How do I choose a style for a hot climate?
Prefer crisp, well attenuated, moderately hopped beers that taste good cold, such as lagers and pale ales.
Do I need a non-alcoholic beer in the range?
Not always. It is worth considering where the market and local law support it.
